scenes.visual: Title: Netrin Guides Growing Axons. Show a developing spinal cord with commissural axons approaching and crossing the ventral midline.

scenes.tts: Netrin is a secreted guidance cue that helps growing axons build connections. In the developing spinal cord, commissural axons grow toward the midline and cross to the other side. Netrin helps guide that journey. In mice lacking netrin, spinal commissural axons take wrong routes, and several forebrain crossings are missing. How does this cue guide the moving tip of an axon, the growth cone?

scenes.visual: Begin with the spinal commissural route toward and across the ventral midline. Label the moving tip growth cone. Compare normal spinal routes with misrouted axons in a mouse lacking netrin-1; in a separate forebrain inset show missing commissures. Keep spinal misrouting distinct from missing forebrain crossings.

scenes.tts: The first clue came from pieces of embryonic rat spinal cord in a gel. A piece of dorsal spinal cord alone sent out few or no axons. Put a piece of floor plate nearby, and axon bundles grew toward it. The pieces never touched. Something crossed the gel. Later, cells made to secrete netrin attracted commissural axons at a distance.

scenes.visual: Show paired collagen-gel assays: dorsal spinal-cord explant alone, with few or no axons; dorsal explant beside a separate floor-plate explant, with commissural axon bundles growing toward it across a visible gap. Then replace floor plate with netrin-secreting cells. Label this culture evidence for attraction at a distance.

scenes.tts: But in the mouse embryo, much of the netrin that matters acts locally. Cells called ventricular zone progenitors make netrin and lay it down on the pial surface, along the axons' path. The growth cone can encounter the cue close to where it is laid down.

scenes.visual: Move from the dish to a mouse embryonic spinal-cord cross-section. Label ventricular-zone progenitors, pial surface and floor plate. Show progenitor-derived netrin deposited along the pial surface beside the commissural axon route. Depict local cue presentation without a smooth, measured long-range concentration field.

scenes.tts: Deleting netrin only from the floor plate left most spinal commissural axons on course. Deleting it from those progenitor cells caused errors. Later studies found that floor plate netrin still contributes, working with progenitor netrin. So the dish shows attraction at a distance. The mouse shows that local netrin matters too, with more than one source helping guide the route.

scenes.visual: Compare control, floor-plate-specific netrin deletion and progenitor-specific netrin deletion in the mouse spinal cord. Keep most routes intact in the floor-plate deletion and show routing errors in the progenitor deletion. Then show both sources contributing to guidance. End on a culture-versus-embryo comparison: distance attraction in gel; substantial local presentation and cooperating sources in mouse. Do not imply floor-plate netrin is dispensable or that all netrin acts only by contact.

scenes.tts: Now ask how the growth cone reads netrin. Receptors on its surface help decide the response. One receptor is called D C C. It usually mediates attraction. Netrin binds cells displaying D C C, and an antibody to D C C blocks netrin evoked outgrowth from spinal cord explants.

scenes.visual: Zoom into a growth cone and label DCC receptors. Illustrate usual attraction toward netrin. Add separate assay insets for netrin binding to DCC-displaying cultured cells and anti-DCC blocking netrin-evoked spinal explant outgrowth; keep binding, outgrowth and directional attraction visually distinct.

scenes.tts: U N C five receptors add repulsion. In worms, forcing this receptor into touch neurons sent their axons away from the cue. The cue stayed the same. Changing the receptor changed the answer. Treat this as a starting point: D C C can also take part in repulsion, and netrin has other receptors and partners.

scenes.visual: Show a worm touch-neuron comparison before and after UNC5 expression, with axons growing away from ventral UNC-6 after expression. Identify UNC-6 as worm netrin. Summarize DCC: usually attraction; UNC5: repulsion, sometimes with DCC. Include a small context note that other receptors and partners also matter; avoid depicting DCC as exclusively attractive.

scenes.tts: One smaller point comes from frog spinal growth cones grown in a dish. Blocking cyclic A M P signalling changed attraction to netrin into repulsion. An antibody to D C C stopped both turns. This is a worked example, not a rule for every axon.

scenes.visual: Label Smaller point: cultured frog spinal growth cones. Show pipette-delivered netrin attracting a growth cone, then repulsion when cAMP signalling is blocked. Show anti-DCC blocking both turns. Close on the scope label: a worked example in this assay, not a universal prediction rule.
End card: Netrin guides growing axons. Local presentation and receptor context shape guidance. No additional spoken summary.
